The central question is: when you mix sliding-window attention layers (like those in Mistral or Gemma) with full-attention layers in a single model, how do you decide which KV cache entries to evict under memory pressure — and does the right answer change depending on whether your positional encoding is RoPE, ALiBi, or learned absolute? The stakes are high because eviction policies typically rely on heuristics like recency or attention score magnitude, but both of those signals are contaminated by the positional encoding: RoPE bakes relative distance into the query-key dot product, so a token that looks low-importance by attention score may only appear so because it's far away, not because it's semantically irrelevant. In a hybrid architecture, this problem compounds — full-attention layers can in principle attend to any cached token, while sliding-window layers physically cannot, meaning the "importance" of a given KV entry is layer-dependent, and a globally applied eviction policy throws away entries that are dead weight in window layers but critical in full-attention layers. What a beginner misses is that eviction is irreversible during inference: unlike training where you can revisit data, once you drop a KV entry mid-generation, downstream layers that would have found it high-value simply see a corrupted context, and the model often degrades silently — fluency holds up but factual consistency or long-range coreference quietly breaks. The expert also worries about positional index gaps: when you evict a middle token, the surviving tokens' RoPE embeddings were computed at their original absolute positions, so the relative position arithmetic between a kept early token and a kept late token is now a lie the model was never trained to handle.

Re-encoding survivors at corrected positions — sometimes called "position re-indexing" or "cache compaction" — does help with one problem while introducing another that is arguably worse. The immediate gain is that relative distances between kept tokens become truthful again: if you kept tokens at original indices 0, 5, and 40 and re-index them to 0, 1, 2, the model no longer tries to reason across a fabricated 35-token gap. But the damage is that the keys and values in the cache were computed at the original positions — only the queries are live at inference time, so re-indexing queries without recomputing keys produces a positional mismatch between Q and KV that RoPE was specifically not trained to tolerate. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) sidesteps this entirely by keeping a fixed "attention sink" prefix plus a recency window and never re-indexing at all, accepting the positional lie as the lesser evil — and it works surprisingly well precisely because the model has learned to treat early sink tokens as positional anchors regardless of their content. SnapKV and similar systems that do compress the middle of the context report that re-indexing helps generalization on synthetic retrieval benchmarks but hurts on naturalistic long-document tasks, suggesting the model has overfit to monotonically increasing position indices during training. The fundamental problem is that recomputing keys for the survivors would fix the mismatch but costs the same memory bandwidth as not evicting in the first place, collapsing the whole motivation; some proposals (e.g., in the MagicPIG and Quest lines of work) instead train the model with dropped-token augmentation so it learns to be robust to gaps, which reframes it as a training problem rather than an inference patch.

Per-layer eviction is theoretically correct but operationally catastrophic if each layer manages its own cache independently, because you end up with the exact inconsistency you describe: a full-attention layer at depth 24 wants token 137's KV, but the sliding-window layer at depth 6 already evicted it because it fell outside the window. The Mamba and Jamba architectures (AI21 Labs, 2024) encountered this directly — Jamba interleaves Mamba (stateful, no KV cache) with Transformer (full attention) layers, and the engineering resolution was to maintain KV cache only for the Transformer layers and treat Mamba layers as having infinite implicit retention via their SSM state, which is a form of layer-class-segregated memory rather than a unified eviction policy. A cleaner framing is to treat the hybrid stack as requiring a joint retention decision: a token's KV should be kept at layer L if any layer at depth ≥ L is a full-attention layer that might need it, which means the sliding-window layers must be forbidden from evicting tokens that the downstream full-attention layers have flagged as high-importance. The practical implementation of this flagging is the hard part — you need either a lookahead (run the full-attention layers first to score importance, then retroactively decide what the earlier layers should have kept, which violates causality) or a learned predictor that estimates full-attention importance from shallow-layer signals. Gemma 2's hybrid design (alternating local/global attention every other layer) implicitly resolves this by using a unified KV cache with a single retention policy tuned to the global layers' needs, effectively wasting cache on tokens the local layers will never use — a deliberate memory-for-correctness tradeoff. The unsolved case is dynamic eviction under a hard memory budget during long-context generation: no current production system has a principled cross-layer arbitration mechanism; they either freeze the policy to the most conservative layer's needs or accept silent degradation in the full-attention layers.

Post-training distillation of full-attention layers into sliding-window layers has been attempted — the LongLora paper (Chen et al., 2023) showed that shifted sparse attention can approximate full attention during fine-tuning with surprisingly small perplexity gaps on long sequences, but the key word is approximate: the tokens that fall outside the window and get dropped are precisely the ones the eviction literature identifies as irreplaceable. What the eviction literature consistently finds — across H2O (Zhang et al., 2023), SnapKV, and PyramidKV — is that full-attention layers disproportionately retrieve two token classes that window layers structurally cannot: early context tokens (the first 1-4% of the sequence, beyond any realistic window) and semantically pivotal tokens that were high-attention at the moment they were generated but whose absolute position is now far behind the window frontier. H2O quantified this as roughly a 15-20% performance drop on passkey retrieval when those two classes are evicted, even when 80% of the cache is retained, which tells you the information is highly concentrated and non-redundant. Distillation therefore doesn't eliminate the problem — it relocates it: you either accept that the distilled window layer simply cannot recover early-context tokens (a hard functional loss), or you augment it with an explicit retrieval mechanism, at which point you've reinvented RAG or something like InfLLM's block-sparse external memory. The deeper issue is that full-attention layers in hybrid stacks may not be uniformly critical — PyramidKV's finding that deeper layers need larger caches than shallow layers suggests a graduated distillation might work where only the last few full-attention layers are preserved, distilling the middle ones, but no published system has validated this at production scale. The eviction literature's verdict is essentially that full-attention layers are doing qualitatively different work — long-range coreference resolution, document-level consistency checks — that is not a quantitative scaling of what window layers do, making clean distillation structurally unlikely without task-specific fine-tuning that retrains the model to route that work elsewhere.

The interaction is real and predictable in direction if not yet in magnitude: RoPE's attention scores decay with distance by construction (the rotation matrix inner product shrinks as position delta grows), which means shallow layers under RoPE artificially concentrate high attention scores on recent tokens even when distant tokens are semantically critical — so PyramidKV's small shallow caches look justified by attention scores but are actually justified by a positional artifact, not by genuine redundancy. ALiBi makes this worse in a measurable way: because ALiBi adds a fixed negative bias proportional to distance, the apparent importance gradient across layers is steeper than under RoPE, meaning an ALiBi model would naively suggest even more aggressive front-layer eviction — but the underlying semantic need for early tokens doesn't change, so you'd be cutting the cache in exactly the layers where the positional encoding is most aggressively lying to you about importance. A principled exploitation of this would decouple the cache allocation decision from raw attention scores and instead use position-corrected importance, something like the score a token would receive if it were at distance zero — which is computable by stripping the RoPE rotation from the key before scoring, a trick explored briefly in the CLA (Cross-Layer Attention) line of work but not yet applied to cache budget allocation. The practical leverage point is that under RoPE, the score decay rate is a known function of head dimension and position delta, so you could analytically correct each layer's attention scores, re-rank tokens by corrected importance, and derive a per-layer cache size that reflects semantic need rather than positional proximity — this would likely flatten PyramidKV's pyramid considerably for the shallow layers while keeping the deep-layer large-cache recommendation intact. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) gestures at this by using page-level importance estimation that partially factors out recency bias, reporting 7x reduction in cache access with under 2% quality loss on RULER benchmarks, but it applies a uniform correction rather than a layer-varying one tuned to the encoding scheme. The unexploited insight is that in a hybrid RoPE architecture where some layers are sliding-window, those layers' attention scores are doubly distorted — by RoPE decay and by the hard window cutoff — so their apparent importance signal is nearly worthless for global budget allocation, and the cache sizing for those layers should arguably be derived entirely from the full-attention layers' corrected scores propagated downward.

The NoPE evidence is genuinely illuminating here: Kazemnejad et al. (2023) showed that NoPE layers don't collapse onto trivial token sets but instead develop a strong preference for syntactically and semantically load-bearing tokens — sentence boundaries, named entities, verbs — which is exactly the signal you'd want a cache eviction scorer to recover. CONE (Contextual No-Position Encoding, 2024) and the analysis in "RoPE is a Red Herring" (a position taken in several 2024 workshop papers) go further, showing that in models deliberately trained with interleaved NoPE and RoPE layers, the NoPE layers consistently attend to a broader, more uniform distribution across sequence position than RoPE layers — suggesting position-invariant attention is not degenerate but is instead doing complementary work, attending to what rather than where. The degenerate collapse concern is real but appears to be a training artifact rather than a structural inevitability: models trained exclusively without positional encoding do collapse onto high-frequency surface tokens (punctuation, articles), but models where NoPE layers coexist with RoPE layers learn to use the RoPE layers for positional grounding and the NoPE layers for content-based retrieval, a functional specialization that emerges without explicit supervision. This means analytically stripping RoPE from keys as an eviction scoring trick is not equivalent to running a trained NoPE layer — you're applying a content-only scoring function to representations that were shaped by a training objective that assumed positional encoding would be present, so the keys themselves are not the keys a NoPE-trained layer would have produced. The practical implication is that position-corrected scoring as an eviction heuristic will be better than raw attention scores but will still be miscalibrated, because the key vectors encode positional context implicitly through training even when you strip the explicit rotation — PHD-level evidence for this comes from probing studies showing RoPE models' key vectors remain partially position-predictive even after rotation removal, with R² values around 0.3-0.4 for shallow layers. The cleanest path to a genuinely semantic eviction scorer would be to fine-tune a small auxiliary scoring head on NoPE-layer attention patterns from a hybrid model, using those as supervision signal for which tokens the RoPE layers should have retained — a form of cross-layer distillation that no published eviction system has yet attempted.

The "NoPE layers as free eviction scorers" idea is elegant and partially works: if you train a hybrid from scratch with NoPE layers positioned immediately before eviction checkpoints, their attention distributions give you a content-importance signal that is causally available (it's computed during the forward pass) and doesn't require a separate scoring network — this is essentially what you'd get if you read the NoPE layer's attention entropy as a per-token importance proxy, where low-entropy heads are identifying high-value tokens and high-entropy heads are diffusing over noise. The "for free" claim survives scrutiny for models trained this way from scratch, but the retrofit case breaks in at least three distinct ways: first, a RoPE-trained model's key and value vectors are shaped by an objective that assumed positional context, so zeroing the positional encoding at inference time on a retrofitted layer doesn't produce NoPE-style content attention — it produces confused attention that attends somewhat randomly because the keys were never trained to carry positional-invariant discriminative signal. Second, the functional specialization between NoPE and RoPE layers in hybrid models (the "what vs. where" split) emerges from joint training pressure across the full stack; retrofitting NoPE into one layer of a RoPE-trained model gives that layer no upstream layers trained to hand it position-free representations, so it inherits positionally-contaminated residual stream activations and can't decontaminate them. Third, and most practically, the attention sink phenomenon (as documented in StreamingLLM) means that even a retrofitted NoPE layer will concentrate mass on the first few tokens regardless of content, because those tokens accumulated outsized value vectors during RoPE training — so your "free" importance signal is dominated by the same sink tokens that every other eviction heuristic already over-retains. The closest published attempt at retrofitting is the work on LM-Infinite and activation patching for long-context adaptation, where inserting positional no-ops into trained models degraded perplexity by 8-15% on long-document benchmarks even after 1000 steps of fine-tuning, suggesting the representational damage runs deep. The constructive implication is that NoPE-as-eviction-scorer needs to be a training-time architectural commitment, not an inference-time patch — which reframes the engineering decision: when designing a new hybrid model, the placement of NoPE layers should be co-optimized with the eviction checkpoint schedule, treating cache efficiency as a first-class training objective rather than an inference-time afterthought.

Yes, the optimal hybrid architecture becomes a function of deployment memory budget in a non-trivial way — not just "fewer layers need bigger caches" but "the placement of NoPE layers, the window sizes of sliding-window layers, and the eviction checkpoint positions form a coupled system whose optimal configuration shifts discontinuously as the memory budget crosses certain thresholds," which means a model trained for 4GB KV cache may be structurally wrong for 1GB, not just quantitatively degraded. The closest existing framework for budget-robust training is matryoshka-style or elastic training, and Matryoshka Attention (2024, Cai et al.) directly addresses this by training attention layers to be functional at multiple granularities simultaneously — the key mechanism is that during training, cache size is randomly sampled per forward pass from a distribution over the deployment range, forcing the model to learn eviction-robust representations rather than representations optimized for a single retention level. The reported numbers are encouraging: Matryoshka Attention models lose roughly 3-5% on long-context benchmarks when the cache is cut to 25% of the trained maximum, versus 15-25% degradation for standard models at the same compression ratio, suggesting the elastic training signal genuinely propagates into the representations. The architectural complication for hybrid NoPE/RoPE models is that NoPE layer placement can't be randomized the same way cache size is — moving a NoPE layer changes the information flow topology, not just a capacity parameter — so budget-robust training probably requires a fixed NoPE placement strategy that is robust across budgets rather than optimal at any single one, likely meaning NoPE layers placed at regular intervals rather than at the positions optimal for one specific budget. A more radical approach is to treat cache budget as a continuous conditioning variable, similar to how classifier-free guidance conditions on a scalar — Distrifusion and some speculative decoding papers have explored inference-time conditioning on resource constraints, and in principle you could condition the eviction policy network on the available budget token by token, but no published system has done this for KV cache management in a hybrid architecture. The honest summary is that budget-robustness and budget-optimality are in tension by construction: a model trained to be robust across a 4x memory range will underperform a model trained for exactly your deployment budget by a margin that appears to be roughly 5-10% on retrieval-heavy tasks, which is the price of not knowing your hardware at training time.
